name: Weir Farm National Historical Park
author: author-C-2026-10-18
summary:
In Branchville, Connecticut, the painter Julian Alden Weir found what he called a “quiet plain little house among the rocks.” He acquired the 153-acre farm in 1882 and for nearly 40 years made it his summer home, building a studio, twice enlarging the house, adding a pond and bringing the land to 238 acres. It inspired Weir and his friends Childe Hassam, John Twachtman and Albert Pinkham Ryder, who painted its stones, woodlands, meadows and pond; after 1890 Weir worked more and more outdoors in an Impressionist style, and in 1897 he, Twachtman and Hassam founded the Ten American Painters. [1]

Accounts of how he got it vary. In June 1882 he wrote that a gentleman had offered him, for a painting he had just bought for $560, the price plus a farm of 150 acres in Connecticut; the historian Hildegard Cummings found that he paid the owners, collector Erwin Davis and his wife Emily, a token ten dollars when the land was deeded to him on July 19, 1882. [2]

Weir’s daughter, the painter Dorothy Weir Young, took over the farm after his death; her husband, sculptor Mahonri Young, built a studio there for his This Is the Place monument, unveiled in 1947. After he died in 1957, painters Sperry and Doris Andrews bought it. With its future uncertain amid 1970s development, a grassroots effort won its designation as a national historic site on October 31, 1990; it became a national historical park on January 5, 2021. About 60 acres remain, with 15 historic structures and hundreds of recorded painting sites; the 2017 foundation document calls it the only place in the park system where much of a landscape integral to several generations of artists remains intact. [1] [3]

labor_ccc.html: Hired farmers and servants did much of the work. For seven years Weir had trouble keeping a reliable farmer; one, a Mr. Holsten, was let go after letting 500 heads of celery, a major cash crop, freeze. Then came Paul Remy, a native of Alsace, who ran the farm with his wife and sons for fifteen years, plowing with oxen, haying and cutting oats. The 1900 census lists the Weir household in Ridgefield with four servants, all single Irish-born women: a cook, waitress, nurse and laundress. Historians Deborah Gardner and Christine McKay write that heavy immigration in the 1880s and 1890s made such help affordable on an artist’s earnings; with no heat, running water or electricity at Branchville in the 1890s, it freed Anna Weir to model for her husband and Ella Weir to travel abroad for months at a time — a reality that, they note, with few early exceptions does not appear in Weir’s art. [2]

sources.title: Gardner and McKay, An Artists’ Retreat — Historic Resource Study (NPS, 2009), “Household and Farm Employees,” pp. 69–71

climate.html: The 2017 foundation document lists climate change among the threats to the landscape the painters recorded: warmer, wetter conditions that make trees and shrubs bloom earlier and change the views, and more extreme rain and heat, flooding, erosion, invasive species and northward shifts in species ranges, all of which it says threaten to alter the cultural landscape. It also warns that the loss of expertise in building dry-stacked stone walls limits the park’s ability to maintain them. [3]
